title: Resting in the Two Turning Points of the Breath
script: This is Door 1. Resting in the two turning points of the breath. It comes from an old Indian text called the Vijnana Bhairava Tantra. The text gives a hundred and twelve ways to rest attention. Each way is called a dharana, which means a place where attention is set. This is verse 24, the first. Here is what it says, in our own plain words. The breath goes up and out, and comes down and in, all by itself. There are two places where these movements begin. Fill those two places with attention, the old text says, and you come to rest in fullness. The verse only says the two places. Later teachers placed them at the heart, where the in-breath ends, and about twelve finger-widths in front of the nose, where the out-breath ends. That placing is their reading. The school follows it. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, or lying on your back, is good too. Choose the one that needs the least effort. Let the floor or the chair carry you completely. Close your eyes lightly, or leave them open, resting on the floor. [pause 4s] Now the two places. One is inside, at the heart. The other is outside, in the air, about twelve finger-widths in front of your nose. Turn your attention toward those two places. Not toward the air itself. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. If counting helps, an even four in and four out. If not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six easy rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] As the in-breath ends, rest your attention at the heart. As the out-breath ends, rest it out in front. The turn is already there. You only meet it. [pause 16s] You may notice the turn is very small. Let it be small. [pause 16s] Now let the counting go. Stay near the two places, lightly. [pause 16s] Take one free breath without watching it. Open the eyes. Carry the sense of fullness into whatever comes next.

title: Not Turning Back from the Two Spaces
script: This is Door 2. Not turning back from the two spaces. It is verse 25 of the old text. Here is what it says, in our plain words. When the breath has gone in, or gone out, there is a small space where it comes to rest. If you don't hurry back from those two spaces, the inner one and the outer one, the old text says the divine shows itself there. The teacher Jaideva Singh says these spaces are tiny natural pauses, one at the heart and one in front of the nose. He says they are only watched. The school follows that reading. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with support under your hips, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take all your weight. There is nothing to keep up. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the two spaces. One is inside, after the in-breath, near the heart. One is outside, after the out-breath, in front of the nose. Face those two spaces. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if you like to count. Each little space lasts exactly as long as it lasts. Don't make it longer. Never force it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] After the in-breath, let attention stay in the inner space. After the out-breath, let it stay in the outer space. Only your attention stays. The breath goes on. [pause 16s] You may notice an urge to rush on into the next breath. Notice it. Let it soften. [pause 16s] Let the counting go now. Breathe your own way. Don't turn back from the spaces too quickly. [pause 20s] Let the breath go unwatched for one round. Open the eyes slowly.

title: The Opened Centre Where Breath Neither Leaves nor Enters
script: This is Door 3. The opened centre, where the breath neither leaves nor enters. It is verse 26 of the old text. In our plain words: when the centre opens, the breath neither goes out nor comes in. Thoughts fall away in that middle. And the old text says the divine appears there. Teachers read this two ways. Some read it as an instruction to stop the breath. Jaideva Singh and Christopher Wallis read it as something that happens by itself when the middle opens. The school follows that second reading. We never stop the breath. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Sit or lie in any easy way. A chair is good. Let the floor or the chair take all your weight. There is no posture to keep. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the middle. It is the quiet join, where the out-breath has ended and the in-breath has not begun. It is more a moment than a place. Turn toward it. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. If it helps you settle, count four in and six out, so the out-breath is a little longer. Six rounds, three at a time. Then we stop counting. [pause 30s] Rest in the quiet join at the end of the out-breath. If the breath pauses there by itself, just watch. Don't lean into it. Don't make it last. [pause 30s] Now stop counting. Let the breath be its own. You may notice thoughts thinning by themselves. Or you may not. Both are fine. [pause 20s] Take one fuller, free breath. Wriggle the fingers. Open the eyes.

title: Retained Breath and the Tranquil
script: This is Door 4. Retained breath and the tranquil. It is verse 27 of the old text. This door is different. The school keeps it as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. Here is what the old text says, in our own plain words. The breath is held, either after it has gone out, or after it has come in. At the end of that holding, the power is called the tranquil, and she shows the Tranquil One. Jaideva Singh explains it the same way: breath kept outside after breathing out, and kept inside after breathing in. That is the history. Listen to it as a story about people long ago. Don't try it from these words. Holding the breath on purpose can bring dizziness or fainting, and it is not right for everyone. The school does not teach it. Anyone who wants to learn it should go only to a qualified teacher, with their own doctor's advice. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 2. Not turning back from the two spaces. There nothing is stopped. You only notice the tiny natural space that is already there, after the breath goes in and after it goes out, and you let it be exactly as long as it is. [pause 3s] Take a normal breath. Look around the room. Move on when ready.

title: Rays Rising from the Root, Dissolving above the Crown
script: This is Door 5. Rays rising from the root, dissolving above the crown. It is verse 28 of the old text. In our plain words: picture a power shining like rays of light from the root. It grows finer, finer than the finest, until it comes to rest at a point above the head. There, the old text says, the divine arises. The verse says only from the root, and at the end of twelve. Jaideva Singh reads the root as the base of the spine, and the end of twelve as a point above the crown. The school follows his reading. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If heat, shaking, restlessness or a strong feeling comes, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with support, is good. Lying down is good. Let your weight settle into what is under you, especially at the base. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the line. It runs from the base of your body, up the centre, to a point just above the crown of your head. Rest your attention at the base first. [pause 3s] Breathe in an ordinary way. About four in and four out, if counting helps. The breath does not push the light. It only goes on, low and easy. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Now imagine a soft light at the base, beginning to rise along the centre line. Nothing moves in the muscles. It is only a picture. [pause 16s] As it rises, it grows finer. Thinner than a thread. Finer still, as it nears the point above the crown. [pause 16s] Let it come to rest above the crown. You may notice the moment it fades. Let the counting go, and stay in the space where it faded. [pause 18s] Let the image go. Feel the weight of the body and the floor. Open the eyes.

title: Lightning Rising Centre by Centre
script: This is Door 6. Lightning rising, centre by centre. It is verse 29 of the old text. In our plain words: picture a power rising like lightning, from one centre to the next, up to about three fists above the head. At the end, the old text says, there is a great dawning. Jaideva Singh explains this as a rising through the centres along the middle of the body, ending three fists above the head. The school teaches only a slow, gentle tracing of it. No rush. No force. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If strong sensations, restlessness, or a strong feeling come, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. If practices with inner energy have shaken you before, choose a breath door or a sound door instead, such as Door 1 or Door 15. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. Let the body be supported and still. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] The map is a line up the middle of the body, with six quiet stations on it. Base. Belly. Heart. Throat. Brow. Crown. And above them, a point about three fists over the head. [pause 3s] Breathe in an ordinary way. About four in and six out, if counting helps. Never use the breath to drive the picture. One breath for each station. Base. [pause 10s] Belly. [pause 10s] Heart. [pause 10s] Throat. [pause 10s] Brow. [pause 10s] Crown. [pause 10s] Now let attention rest in the open space above the head. Let the counting go. [pause 18s] Let the image go. Feel the feet and the floor. Open the eyes.

title: Twelve Stations, Twelve Letters
script: This is Door 7. Twelve stations, twelve letters. It is verse 30 of the old text. In our plain words: there are twelve stations, one above another, each marked by a letter. Attend to each one, first plainly, then finely, then in its highest form, and leave each behind in turn. At the end, the old text says, is Shiva, its name for the divine. The verse itself names neither the stations nor the letters. Those lists come from later teachers. The school uses a short, simple form: six stations up the middle of the body, and no letters. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. Let the body be supported. The climb is only in attention. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] The six stations are the pelvic floor, the navel, the heart, the throat, the brow, and the crown. At each one, feel it plainly. Then feel a finer quiet there. Then leave it, and rise. [pause 3s] Even breath. Four in, four out, if counting helps. Quiet and even. One breath for each station. The pelvic floor. [pause 8s] The navel. [pause 8s] The heart. [pause 8s] The throat. [pause 8s] The brow. [pause 8s] The crown. [pause 8s] Now there is nothing to climb. Let the counting go. You may notice the letting go itself, each time a station was left. [pause 15s] Let the ladder go. Rest one breath at the top in open space. Open the eyes.

title: Filling to the Crown, Crossing the Brow-Bridge
script: This is Door 8. Filling to the crown, crossing the brow-bridge. It is verse 31 of the old text. The school keeps this door as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. Here is the old teaching, in our plain words. Quickly fill the body with breath-power, up to the top of the head. Break through by a bridge made by drawing the eyebrows together. Make the mind free of thought. Then, in what is above all, the all-pervading arises. Jaideva Singh wrote that the real method of the brow-bridge was a closely guarded secret, and is now practically lost. Some readers also take the breaking through to mean stopping the breath. So we leave it where it is, in memory. Forcing the breath in fast, stopping it, and squeezing the brow can bring headache or dizziness. Don't attempt them from words. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 3. The opened centre. There you only rest in the quiet middle between the out-breath and the in-breath, where thoughts may thin by themselves. Nothing is forced, and the breath is never stopped. [pause 3s] Take an easy breath. Relax the forehead. Move on when ready.

title: The Five Voids of the Peacock Feather
script: This is Door 9. The five voids of the peacock feather. It is verse 32 of the old text. In our plain words: meditate on five empty circles, like the rings of colour in a peacock's feather. That way, the old text says, you enter the heart, the deepest emptiness. Jaideva Singh reads the five as the five senses: sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell. The school follows his reading. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If the senses feel like too much, open your eyes and look at one simple thing in the room. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. Let the body be supported and still. If you have a peacock feather, or a picture of one, look at it softly for a moment. Then close your eyes. [pause 6s] The map is the eye of the feather. Rings of colour, around one dark, empty centre. Place that centre at your heart. [pause 3s] Even, natural breath. About four in and four out. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Notice the senses as rings. Sight and sound on the outside. Touch, taste and smell inside them. [pause 16s] Let the rings narrow, slowly, toward the quiet centre at the heart. Don't chase any sensation. [pause 16s] Let the counting go. Rest near that empty centre. There is nothing to make happen. [pause 18s] Open the eyes. Let the senses come back one by one: sound, light, touch.

visual.concept: The eye of a peacock feather drawn as five soft concentric rings around a dark empty centre at the heart position; the rings narrow slowly toward the centre while a faint pulse keeps the 4-in, 4-out count.

title: Attention Dissolving into Space, a Wall, or a Worthy Vessel
script: This is Door 10. Attention dissolving into space, a wall, or a worthy vessel. It is verse 33 of the old text. In our plain words: wherever your attention rests, on empty space, on a wall, or on a worthy vessel, it melts there by itself, and that is a gift. Worthy vessel is read in different ways. Jaideva Singh reads it as a good and able person, a pupil. Others read it another way. Here we use the plainest supports: a blank wall, or open sky. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Blink whenever you need to. Don't stare until your eyes strain. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Sit where you can see a plain wall or open sky. A chair is good. Let the body be supported, so nothing pulls you away. [pause 4s] Choose one support. The wall, or the sky. Let your gaze rest on it, soft and steady. That one place is all there is to do. [pause 4s] Natural breath. About four in, four out, if counting helps. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Keep your attention on the support. If a thought comes, let it pass. Don't follow it. [pause 16s] Let your attention melt into what it rests on, a little more each breath. [pause 16s] Let the counting go. Stay with the wall or the sky. Blink when you need to. [pause 18s] Look away from the support. Take in the whole room. Move on when ready.

title: Mind Placed Inside the Skull
script: This is Door 11. Mind placed inside the skull. It is verse 34 of the old text. In our plain words: stay with your eyes closed, and place your mind inside the skull. As the mind slowly steadies, the old text says, you perceive the highest thing there is to perceive. Most translators say inside the skull. Some teachers place it at the crown of the head. The school uses the whole space inside the head. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If your head feels pressure, or starts to ache, move your attention down to the breath at the belly, or open your eyes and stop. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Sit or lie in any steady way. A chair is good. Let the body be still and supported, the head balanced without effort. Close your eyes. The verse asks for that. [pause 4s] Now the space inside your skull. Feel it as a soft bowl of space. Not a tight point. Rest your attention there. [pause 3s] Natural, even breath. About four in and four out. Keep the throat soft. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Rest in the space inside the head. Soft, like light filling a bowl. [pause 16s] Steadiness grows bit by bit, if it grows. Don't force a vision. Don't force a blank. [pause 16s] Let the counting go. Stay in the bowl of space, lightly. [pause 18s] Let attention drop to the breath at the belly. Open the eyes slowly.

title: Space Within the Central Channel
script: This is Door 12. Space within the central channel. It is verse 35 of the old text. In our plain words: in the middle of the body there is a channel, as thin as the fine thread inside a lotus stalk. Meditate on it as open inner sky, and through it, the old text says, the divine shines. The verse says only in the middle. Jaideva Singh calls this the central channel. The school follows his reading. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If the picture brings strong sensations or restlessness, open your eyes and feel your whole body resting on the floor. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. Let the body be supported. There is no lifting of the spine. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the channel. One very fine line through the exact middle of your body, from the base to the crown. Thinner than a hair. Feel the inside of it as open space. Not a muscle to grip. [pause 3s] Equal breath, four in and four out, if counting helps. Otherwise natural. The channel is felt, not breathed into. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Rest in the fine line through the middle. [pause 16s] Feel the space inside it. Quiet. Open. [pause 16s] Let the counting go. Stay with the quiet of that inner space. [pause 18s] Let the channel go. Feel the whole body again. Open the eyes.

title: Sealing the Sense-Doors, Watching the Point Dissolve
script: This is Door 13. Sealing the sense-doors, watching the point dissolve. It is verse 36 of the old text. The school keeps this door as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. The old text says, in our plain words: close the doors of the senses with the hands, and pierce the point between the eyebrows. A point of light is seen. As it slowly dissolves, in its middle is the highest state. Jaideva Singh describes the old hand seal. The thumbs close the ears. The fingers cover the eyes, and close the nostrils and the mouth. He also tells that Swami Lakshmanjoo taught it the other way round: the point of light first, the seal after. Because the old seal covers the eyes and closes the nose and mouth, the school does not teach it. Never press on the eyes. Never block the nose or the mouth. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 1. Resting at the two turning points of the breath. This verse has no direct practice door in the school, so Door 1 is a good place to begin. There you only notice where the breath turns, at the heart and just in front of the nose. Nothing is forced, and the breath is never stopped. [pause 3s] Open the eyes fully. Look around the room. Move on when ready.

title: The Point of Subtle Fire
script: This is Door 14. The point of subtle fire. It is verse 37 of the old text. The school keeps this door as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. The old text says, in our plain words: meditate on a tiny point, like a spark of subtle fire, at the top of the head or in the heart. Watch it until it dissolves, and then the dissolving itself dissolves. In the old reading, the spark came from pressing or stirring the eyes. Jaideva Singh also gives another reading: the sparks seen as a lamp goes out. Because the old way uses pressure on the eyes, the school keeps this door as memory. Never press or rub the eyes to make light. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 10. Attention dissolving into space, a wall, or a worthy vessel. There your eyes rest softly on a plain wall or open sky, untouched, and attention melts into what it rests on. [pause 3s] Open the eyes and look at something far away. Move on when ready.

title: Bathing in the Unstruck Sound
script: This is Door 15. Bathing in the unstruck sound. It is verse 38 of the old text. In our plain words: there is a sound that nothing strikes. It runs without a break, rushing like a river, heard by an ear that is ready. One who bathes in it, the old text says, reaches the highest. Jaideva Singh says it is an inner sound. Some teachers compare it to a waterfall. The verse itself says only that it is unbroken, like a river. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If listening inward makes a ringing in your ears feel upsetting, stop, and listen to ordinary sounds in the room instead. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. Let the body be supported and still. Close your eyes. [pause 4s] Now the sound. If it helps, begin with a steady sound near you: running water, wind, or a fan. That is your stream. If you like, rest your palms lightly over your ears. Never press. [pause 4s] Natural, quiet breath. About four in and six out, if counting helps. Let the breath stay quieter than the listening. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 20s] Listen to the steady outer sound. Let it flow, like a river. [pause 20s] Now listen underneath it, for the faint, steady hum heard when a room is quiet. If you don't hear one, stay with the outer stream. That is fine. [pause 20s] Let the counting go. Don't study the sound. Bathe in it. [pause 18s] Let ordinary sounds come back. Open the eyes slowly.

title: Praṇava Fading into Void
script: This is Door 16. Pranava fading into void. It is verse 39 of the old text. In our plain words: sound a sacred syllable fully, such as Om, and let its sound stretch long. At the end of the long sound, rest in the emptiness that is left. Through that emptiness, the old text says, you reach emptiness itself. The old word for such a syllable is pranava. Teachers name Om, and also Hum and Hrim. We will use Om. If you have been taught another, you may use that one. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Keep the sound soft. Stop before the breath feels short. If you feel light-headed, go back to ordinary breathing. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. Let the body relax. Jaw and throat soft. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the place to rest. It is the moment the sound ends, and the quiet just after it. [pause 3s] Breathe in easily, for about four. Then let the out-breath carry a long, soft Om, for about eight. Aloud, or silently inside. If eight is too long, make the sound shorter and let the breath simply finish. Never strain. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 24s] When the sound ends, stay right there in the quiet. The next in-breath will come by itself. Don't wait for it. Don't stop it. [pause 24s] Don't reach for the next thought, or the next sound. [pause 24s] Now let the sound rest. Stay with the silence it left. [pause 15s] Breathe normally for a few rounds. Open the eyes.

visual.concept: One horizontal wave carried on the out-breath that tapers to a thin line and then to blank space, the silence; on each in-breath a soft point gathers at the left. Timed 4 in, 8 out.

elements.description: Full-frame dark field, deep night blue (#0A0F1E). Nothing else lives in the background.
A soft gold point (#F2D8A0) at the left of the frame that gathers light on the in-breath.
A horizontal gold wave that flows right on the out-breath, tapering from full height to a thin line.
The open dark space at the right where the line ends: the quiet after the sound.
